messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Jabari was seven years old when he watched his father beat his mother in their living room. He remembers it not as a story but as a series of snapshots: the sharp crack of the first slap, his mother’s eyes widening in disbelief, the way his father’s silhouette loomed against the window. He stood frozen in the doorway, his body locked in a posture he would later recognize as the same one that returned in moments of sudden touch or silence. He couldn’t move, couldn’t call out, and afterward he told himself he should have done something—a thought that burrowed into him and stayed.

That feeling of helplessness shaped the years that followed. He began avoiding places he didn’t know, because he couldn’t assess the danger there. Silence made his stomach tighten; he felt sure something bad was about to happen. He started noticing objects that could be used as weapons—a beer bottle on a table, a screwdriver left on a counter—and scanning for them before anything else. His mother eventually left his father, but for Jabari the threat never really left.

At eighteen, he became a police officer—a job that, he thought, would let him be the one who acted instead of the one who froze. Instead, it put him directly in the path of his triggers every day. Patrolling a quiet residential block at dusk, the unusual silence would press against his ears, and the snapshot memory of that living room would flash: his mother’s face, his father’s arm. That memory, in turn, made him scan more intently for weapons, confirming his sense that danger was near. He came to believe that his reactions since the event meant he was going crazy—a thought that made every minor discomfort, a person acting suspiciously or an unexpected touch on the shoulder, feel like a warning signal of imminent collapse.

One afternoon, a colleague clapped him on the back in a briefing room. Jabari’s body instantly locked—the same frozen posture from when he was seven—and the snapshot of his mother’s eyes returned with a wave of grief so sharp he had to excuse himself. The memory reinforced his belief that he couldn’t rely on himself; if a friendly pat could incapacitate him, how could he handle a real threat? That self-doubt drove him to check every corner, every shadow, every unfamiliar street, and the more he checked, the more he noticed potential weapons and suspicious movements, which triggered new memories and deepened his sense that he was losing control.

The cycle tightened over weeks. His hypervigilance turned ordinary interactions into triggers: a shopper acting oddly made him replay the moment his father’s hand connected; the hush in an elevator brought back the silence before the first blow. Each trigger revived the memory, and each memory strengthened his helplessness. He began avoiding unfamiliar parts of his beat, asking for reassignment to the same two blocks he knew, but even there he couldn’t shake the feeling that he was about to be caught off guard.

What finally brought him to seek help was a night when he pulled over a car for a minor infraction. The driver’s sudden movement toward the glove box made Jabari’s mind go blank—he later realized he had frozen, just like when he was seven, while his hand rested inches from his service weapon. He drove home shaking, certain he was going crazy, unable to trust himself on duty. In the clinic, he said he wasn’t sure what he was most afraid of: that he would freeze again, or that he would finally stop caring and react the wrong way. Either way, he wanted the snapshots to stop.

violation_explanations: No paragraph conveys that a sense of threat leads to or triggers the trauma memory; instead, memories are triggered by external cues or by negative appraisals.
